title: Where do you work?
goal: Get your sentences moving with real verbs. Three groups, eighteen endings, and one simple way to guess the group of any new verb you meet.

dialogs.title: Диалог — After class
dialogs.intro: Ivan and Ani are chatting in the university corridor. All the verbs in this dialogue are in the present tense; watch the endings, because three different patterns appear side by side.

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: I don't work yet. I study Bulgarian at the university.
lines.literal: still — not — work-I. study-I — Bulgarian — in — university-the.

lines.speaker: Иван:
lines.id: How many hours a day do you study?

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: Three or four. In the morning I read, and in the afternoon I write exercises.
lines.literal: three — or — four. mornings — read-I, and — afternoon — write-I — exercises.

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: Not everything. When people speak fast, I don't understand.
lines.literal: not — everything. when — people-the — speak-they — fast, not — understand-I.

lines.speaker: Иван:

lines.speaker: Иван:
lines.id: Very much. The kids ask interesting things.

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: So we both work — you with children, me with grammar!

notes: **The dictionary form of a Bulgarian verb is the "I" form, not a base form.** The dictionary lists *работя* (I work), not "to work". The reason is simple: Bulgarian **has no infinitive at all** — there's no form equivalent to "to work" standing on its own. Unit 8 is all about how the language lives without it.

**Pronouns can be dropped, and usually are.** *Работя* already means "I work" without *аз*. The ending already tells you who's doing it, so *аз* is used only for emphasis. ⚠️ English speakers tend to put a pronoun in every sentence because English requires it; here that habit makes your speech sound heavy.

**Сутрин, следобед, вечер are used without a preposition.** *Сутрин чета* — in the morning I read. No *в* or *на* needed. These forms already work as time expressions, like English "mornings, I read".

**Работата си means "one's own job".** The word **си** is used when the owner is the same as the subject of the sentence. *Обичаш ли работата си?* — do you like **your own** job? With *ти* the meaning changes: *Обичам работата ти* — I like **your** job. ⚠️ The practical rule: if owner = subject, use *си*.
**Когато means "when" in statements; кога means "when?" in questions.** *Кога работиш?* (When do you work?) vs *Когато работя…* (When I work…). Similar pairs: *къде / където*, *какво / каквото*.

**Неща is the irregular plural of нещо** (thing, something). Bulgarian has a small group of neuter nouns whose plural ends in -а with a sound change: *нещо → неща*, *дете → деца*, *име → имена*. Learn them as you meet them; there aren't many.
**И двамата means "both of us" or "both of you".** The *и* here isn't "and" but "also, both". *Двамата* uses the special number for people you learned in Unit 5, this time with the article.

grammars.title: The three verb groups
body: Every Bulgarian verb uses one of three sets of endings. What decides it is **the last vowel before the ending in the "he/she" form**: -е means Group I, -и means Group II, -а means Group III.
after: Notice that the *аз* and *те* forms look alike in all groups (**-а/-я** and **-ат/-ят**); what really sets them apart are the four forms in the middle. If you know the *ти* form of a verb, you automatically know its whole group.

**Group III is the biggest and the most regular.** Every verb whose dictionary form ends in **-ам** or **-ям** belongs here without exception: *имам, искам, питам, разбирам, преподавам, плащам, работя*… ⚠️ except the last one. *Работя* ends in -я and belongs to Group II: *работиш, работи*.

grammars.title: Negation: one word, one place
body: To make a verb negative, put **не** right in front of it. No helper verb, no change to the verb. This is one of the easiest parts of all Bulgarian.
after: ⚠️ The only exception is *имам*, whose negative fuses into **нямам** — you learned it in Unit 4.
In speech, **не** pulls the stress onto itself and the verb after it loses its stress: *не рабОтя* is said almost as one word, *NEH-ra-bo-tya*. That makes negation easy to hear even in fast speech.

sections.title: Thirty verbs that cover everyday conversation

blocks.text: Arranged by group, so you know the endings straight away. The forms listed are dictionary forms ("I").

⚠️ Two Group I verbs are highly irregular and are best learned whole right now: **ям** (eat) → *ям, ядеш, яде, ядем, ядете, ядат*, and **мога** (can) → *мога, можеш, може, можем, можете, могат*. You'll use both every day.

sections.title: Times of day and how often

blocks.text: ⚠️ **Никога demands a double negative.** *Никога не работя вечер* — literally "never not work-I evening", meaning "I never work in the evening". Dropping *не* makes the sentence wrong, not shorter. This pattern applies to the whole family of negative words and is covered in full in Unit 13.

Frequency words usually stand **before the verb**: *Често чета вечер.* But Bulgarian is fairly relaxed about word order; moving them to the end doesn't make the sentence wrong, it just shifts the emphasis.
